texto: Odin, king of the gods, has only one eye. What happened to the other?
He did not lose it in a fight. The Norse poems tell something different.
They say he gave it away himself, in exchange for wisdom.
It is the most famous price any god ever paid.
The world tree, Yggdrasil, has three enormous roots.
Under one of them, in the land of the giants, lies a well.
It is Mímir's well. Whoever drinks its water becomes wise.
According to Snorri, an Icelandic poet and historian, the well holds wisdom and hidden knowledge.
The well has a guardian: Mímir, a being of great wisdom.
According to the Völuspá, Mímir drinks mead every morning, and that is why he knows so much.
He is the same Mímir whose head advises Odin. We already told how he lost it.
Mímir did not give his water away. Every sip had a price.
Odin wanted to know everything: what was, what is, and what will be.
He knew the end of the world, Ragnarök, was coming, and he wanted to be ready.
So he traveled alone to the well, wrapped in his cloak and hat.
He asked for a drink. Mímir told him the price.
The price was an eye. Odin did not hesitate.
The poem Völuspá says: 'I know, Odin, where you hid your eye, in Mímir's famous well.'
He left the eye at the bottom of the water, as a pledge for his wisdom.
He drank from the well, and the world opened before his mind.
From that day he saw the future, though it brought him no peace.
For the Norse, it was an enormous price, and still worth paying.
Odin paid one eye but gained a deeper sight.
That is why in art he wears a patch, or a hat brim over his face.
His ravens Huginn and Muninn tell him what they see, so he sees more than any god.
The poems leave a mysterious detail: Odin's eye is still in the well.
Snorri writes that Odin left his eye there as a pledge for the drink.
The Völuspá says Mímir drinks each morning 'from the pledge of the Father of the Slain'.
Many readers think that pledge is the eye, but the poems do not explain it.
When Ragnarök comes, the Völuspá says Odin will speak once more with Mímir's head.
He will know what awaits him, and still he will fight.
That is Odin's greatness: knowing the end and never giving up.
It all began with an eye left in a well, on an ordinary day.
Odin gave up part of himself to see further. The Norse admired those who could sacrifice.
And in those poems, wisdom always costs something.
What would you give in exchange for knowing everything? Tell us in the comments.
